entities.name: Bartolomeo da Rinonico
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Bartolomeo da Rinonico, also known as Bartholomew of Pisa, was a pivotal Italian Franciscan friar and hagiographer whose monumental work, *De conformitate vitae beati Francisci ad vitam Domini Iesu*, profoundly shaped the self-understanding and external perception of the Franciscan Order in the late 14th century. Born in Pisa, Italy, his life culminated with his death on November 4, 1401. Rinonico's magnum opus, completed around 1385, was a systematic and extensive comparison of the life of Saint Francis of Assisi to that of Jesus Christ, asserting Francis as a unique 'alter Christus' and solidifying the spiritual authority and distinctiveness of the Friars Minor during a period of internal strife and external criticism within the Church.

The *De conformitate* meticulously cataloged parallels between Francis's life and the Gospels, organizing them into four books corresponding to the four Gospels, and further subdividing them into distinct 'conformities.' This encyclopedic undertaking, drawing on a vast array of Franciscan hagiography, miracles, and historical accounts, served as both a spiritual treatise and a defense of the Franciscan ideal. It provided a comprehensive narrative framework for understanding Francis's sanctity, emphasizing his stigmata and his role as a living embodiment of Christ's virtues. The work was widely disseminated within the order, becoming a foundational text for Franciscan spirituality, preaching, and identity.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Bartolomeo da Rinonico's *De conformitate* was a foundational text for the Franciscan Order, solidifying its spiritual identity and sparking theological debates across Europe regarding the nature of sanctity. His work profoundly influenced the perception of Saint Francis as an 'alter Christus' for centuries.
